item.title: CLOSEDQUORUM: Malware Puts AI in the C2 Loop
item.description:
CLOSEDQUORUM is the first publicly documented Windows implant to replace human C2 tasking with a commercial LLM voting panel, delegating tactical attack decisions to DeepSeek, Qwen, Mistral, and Google Gemini in sequence.
Key findings:
- The implant is a 16.4 MB, 64-bit Go executable discovered by Cisco Talos through its CAIRN project. At initialization it collects hostname, OS architecture, CPU count, Windows version, privilege status, and current target process, then sends that host context to up to four LLM providers. Each model returns a structured JSON response selecting the next action. Plurality vote wins. Ties resolve deterministically by provider order: DeepSeek, then Qwen, then Mistral, then Gemini. If all providers fail, the implant sleeps and retries rather than defaulting to a capability.
- The LLM decision layer selects from a constrained action set. "steal" triggers simultaneous LSASS credential dumping, saved credential theft from Chrome, Edge, and Firefox, and cryptocurrency wallet theft from MetaMask, Exodus, and Ethereum stores. Stolen data is encrypted with AES-256-GCM and exfiltrated via Discord webhook. "inject" invokes shellcode and routes to either process hollowing or Early Bird APC injection. "persist" invokes persistence routines, and Talos identifies WMI persistence creation as a correlatable behavior. A "move" decision exists in the schema but has no implemented handler in the analyzed build.
- The publicly distributed binary is an inert template with placeholder LLM API keys and a dummy Discord webhook. Talos assesses the operating model as a configurable service: operators compile a custom build with their own credentials before deployment, and stolen credentials flow back through their Discord channel, effectively a credentials-as-a-service offering with autonomous LLM orchestration as the differentiator. Developer artifacts link to criminal-forum carding activity dating to 2025. No confirmed in-the-wild deployment has been observed.
- The architectural significance is the effort displacement model. The LLMs are not writing exploits or inventing attack paths. They are choosing among predefined capabilities the developer already coded, using host context as input. This removes the human operator from a bounded decision loop and allows the implant to continue executing while the attacker is offline. The same pattern is extensible to other intrusion phases, and it routes all C2 traffic through legitimate commercial AI infrastructure rather than attacker-controlled domains or IPs, putting pressure on detections that depend on known-bad destinations.
Six SHA-256 hashes are listed in the report: 250d4fa37488af9b025333fa17705573d721467b203765bc360890b4f5a90cd7, c4dc171f2513fcaf9d5ecc815a94aee4063b213ab380f80bd3ac422dee5205a7, c13cea04f598e2b0c248d603a6e31bd13aabb64d8149c1b6a77b64e0b983a86f, f5f1f8c3e7b883793800ab6ccf21b3e60bd0730f300b4595fe74a33adc17a63c, 5191cf625dfc209a347f137b50aea199e82040fd5ee9086fb3e2de73c133f3cb, and eddbd0ecf7195d38fefae5b9d393abfa79e6f3f94bde19308ecef130a05a42e5.
Hunt for Go-compiled 64-bit executables making outbound HTTPS to LLM provider API endpoints alongside concurrent Discord webhook POST traffic. Correlate with LSASS access events, WMI subscription creation, and process hollowing indicators such as a spawned suspended process followed by WriteProcessMemory and ResumeThread calls. Wallet and browser credential paths in AppData are the on-disk artifacts to triage. The implant's LLM dependency also means API key strings embedded in a binary are a detection surface worth adding to your triage playbook.

item.title: Detections Digest #20260928
item.description:
Weekly detection engineering roundup: 80 new rules and 43 updates across 11 repositories cover RMM abuse, LSASS dumping, email evasion, BYOVD, and Kubernetes container threats from Sep 21-28, 2026.
Key findings this week:
- RMM abuse detection expanded significantly via magicsword-io/LOLRMM and RussianPanda95/Yara-Rules, with 41 new rules covering process creation, file artifacts, registry persistence under Run keys and service installation paths, and outbound network connections for tools including Zecurit, Allocentra, OpenDesk, RMMCRAT, BlackCrypt, LightRmmAgent, and RemoteAgentAgent. A new YARA rule for RMMCRAT specifically targets PE headers combined with embedded RMMC and RMM Agent configuration strings. The generic DNS rule covering known RMM infrastructure was also refreshed with updated domain and IP indicators. Hunt for agent binaries in AppData, ProgramData, and Program Files alongside Run key writes and outbound DNS to unfamiliar cloud hosting endpoints.
- LSASS and token access detections in splunk/security_content and SigmaHQ/sigma moved from static GrantedAccess string matching to bitwise evaluations against Sysmon Event ID 10 telemetry. This matters because minor mask variations broke prior rules. Updated rules now cover read permissions on lsass.exe, Winlogon duplicate handle access, WMI token impersonation via wmiprvse.exe, and injection into notepad.exe. The Dumpert LSASS dumper detection shifted to IMPHASH-based matching rather than MD5 or command-line paths, which are trivially modified. Cross-reference Sysmon Event ID 10 bitwise access masks with process lineage and file_path fields for Task Manager dump artifacts.
- Email evasion coverage in sublime-security/sublime-rules received 12 new and 12 updated rules. New detections parse .ics calendar invites with oversized guest lists carrying voicemail, purchase order, missed call, and BEC lures, and decode hex-obfuscated recipient strings embedded in URL fragments and QR codes across PDF, ICS, and image attachments. Rules also flag Google Cloud Storage links to short HTML paths, newly registered domains on suspicious TLDs serving single-character HTML files, client-side JavaScript beaconing visitor tokens via dynamic Image objects, and Teams help desk impersonation correlated with mail bombing within a one-hour window. Updated rules unwrap Mimecast-protected links and refresh Spamhaus ASN-DROP coverage, removing prefixes tied to AS63023 and AS62563.
- BYOVD and in-memory defense evasion coverage updated across magicsword-io/LOLDrivers, rabbitstack/fibratus, and kevoreilly/CAPEv2. LOLDrivers rules added MD5, SHA1, SHA256, and IMPHASH values alongside driver filenames in ImageLoaded telemetry to catch hypervisor-protected code integrity bypasses. Four Fibratus rules for process hollowing, ghostly hollowing, activation context manipulation, and NTDLL remapping via file mapping were updated for engine version 3.2.0, refining section type filters including IMAGE and IMAGE_NO_EXECUTE. A new YARA rule in CAPEv2 detects Defendnot, a tool that impairs Windows Defender, via PE magic bytes and characteristic debug strings.
- Kubernetes container threat detection expanded through benscha/KQLAdvancedHunting with 13 new KQL rules querying CloudProcessEvents and CloudAuditEvents in Microsoft Defender XDR. Coverage includes reverse shells using network redirection, XMRig and Kinsing cryptominer execution, first-seen container binary baselining, container escape via nsenter, chroot, unshare, and socket interaction, service account token and ca.crt file reads, Kubernetes secret enumeration across namespaces, cluster-admin role binding creation, and deployment from unapproved registries. GitOps controllers ArgoCD and Flux are excluded to reduce noise. A new jkerai1 rule monitors AzureActivity for modifications to Azure public and private DNS zones, a low-visibility path adversaries use for traffic redirection.
Practitioner takeaway: the shift from static hash and string matching to bitwise access mask evaluation in LSASS rules is the most operationally significant change this week, since it closes a known evasion gap. Prioritize pulling updated Sysmon Event ID 10 rules from splunk/security_content and SigmaHQ/sigma into your pipeline. For RMM hunting, stack process, file path, registry, and network rules together rather than running them in isolation: a single layer is easy to miss, four correlated layers is a detection story. Full rule sets, IOCs, and YARA content are available in the linked repositories.

item.title: NeedyMantis: Unpacking a post-compromise malware family used in targeted operations
item.description:
NeedyMantis is a modular, post-compromise C++ and shellcode framework linked to Chinese 🇨🇳 threat actors, hitting telecoms, universities, and government contractors since at least October 2025.
- Storm-3069 is the named operator Microsoft associates with NeedyMantis, tied to the DAEMON Tools supply chain compromise previously reported by Kaspersky. Microsoft has not attributed Storm-3069 to a Chinese 🇨🇳 nation-state but notes all observed activity aligns with Chinese 🇨🇳 interests and selective deployment patterns. Additional NeedyMantis activity beyond Storm-3069 suggests more than one operator may have access to the framework.
- The delivery chain starts with DLL sideloading: a malicious first-stage loader masquerades as a legitimate DLL (WinSparkle.dll, libcurl.dll, vim64.dll, dbghelp.dll, jli.dll, nvml.dll) dropped alongside real software such as Poedit, curl, Vim, or TightVNC. The archive holding the payloads uses a custom XOR-encoded, RtlDecompressBuffer-compressed file format with per-sample offsets and keys. One observed incident used Impacket to copy the malicious bundle from a network share and execute it on a target host. The first-stage loader SHA-256 is e842dd7642c8e04b5ec20b6393848a9c904e4832930950c16664fe7800ba382e, and the WinSparkle archive is 9cb68f986043a576e19d32184c583b7d8f571c7219d8dc0065dced1c13f077ef.
- A file named encryptbase64.ps1 (actually x64 shellcode despite the extension) serves as the second-stage loader, decoding an embedded payload using ROR-based API hashing with rotation value 11. The main component loads configuration from a file named dnsapi.dll (not the real Windows DLL) and the communications module from ws2_32.dll (also fake). C2 is corp.tripswithengine[.]com on port 443 via URI /library/zip/. The initial beacon is an HTTPS GET where system information (hostname, username, process list, ProgramFiles contents) is Base64 and RtlCompressBuffer-encoded into a Set-Cookie header. The session upgrades to WebSockets, then a binary protocol with RC4 encryption keyed from a 1024-byte random buffer exchanged at handshake. The hard-coded user-agent is firefox/21.0, a reliable hunt anchor.
- The main component creates a mutex formatted as username-processname (e.g., Contoso-Poedit.exe) and supports dynamic module loading and unloading via commands 1020 and 1030, making the full capability set unknown until modules are recovered from operator infrastructure. Config, communications, and shellcode loader are all stored inside the custom archive as files with spoofed Windows system DLL names.
Hunt priority: query for the spoofed DLL paths (WinSparkle.dll in Poedit dirs, libcurl.dll under ProgramData\USOShared, vim64.dll under ProgramData\VIM or TightVNC\VIM, dbghelp.dll under ProgramData\office or broadcom, jli.dll under ProgramData\Intel, nvml.dll under ProgramFiles\modifiable or ProgramData\ics), outbound connections or any log entries referencing corp.tripswithengine[.]com, and user-agent string firefox/21.0 in proxy and firewall logs. The mutex pattern username-processname is a host-based artifact worth sweeping for. Microsoft's report includes KQL hunting queries for Defender XDR and Sentinel, plus the full IOC table and Microsoft Defender Antivirus detections (TrojanDropper:Win64/NeedyMantis, Behavior:Win64/NeedyMantis).

item.title: Quarantined isn't contained: Agentic phishing response with Elastic and Sublime
item.description:
Siloed email and endpoint alerts let phishing campaigns hide in plain sight. An agentic integration between Elastic and Sublime Security closes that gap, correlating quarantine events with endpoint telemetry and enabling bidirectional response without tool-switching.
Key findings:
- The core visibility problem is timing and context. A Sublime Security quarantine at 9:00 a.m. and a suspicious PowerShell process at 9:05 a.m. on the same host each look benign in isolation. Neither tool sees the other's signal, so the campaign opener goes uninvestigated. The native Elastic integration pulls Sublime telemetry (what was flagged, why, who was targeted, and what Sublime did) into Elastic Security alongside endpoint, identity, and network data, letting detection rules run across the combined dataset rather than each half separately.
- Attack Discovery acts as the agentic first pass. Once alerts stack up, Attack Discovery correlates them into unified attack chains by hunting for related activity, reading individual alerts, checking entity context, and querying raw logs across the platform. The output is a prioritized, evidence-grounded account of what happened, mapped to MITRE ATT&CK, with the reasoning visible to the analyst, not a raw queue to triage.
- The bidirectional SOAR integration is the containment multiplier. If Elastic Defend identifies malware on a host, a workflow can take that file's SHA-256 hash and trigger a blast-radius quarantine back in Sublime Security, pulling the same indicator from every mailbox it reached. The response flows from endpoint finding to email-side containment without leaving Elastic. The reverse also applies: a Sublime quarantine event can seed an Elastic case and push a Slack notification with the supporting evidence already attached for analyst review.
- Human-in-the-loop controls are per-action, not system-wide. Elastic Workflows lets teams set the automation threshold at the individual action level. A blast-radius mailbox quarantine, which is high-impact and difficult to reverse, routes through analyst approval. Low-impact enrichment or tagging steps can run automatically. The recommended approach is to start with maximum human review, compare the agentic recommendations against analyst judgment over time, and expand automation incrementally as trust builds.
Practitioner takeaway: The rollout path matters. Stage one is getting Sublime telemetry flowing into Elastic so existing detection rules immediately gain email context with no workflow changes required. Stage two is enabling the bidirectional SOAR actions after you have decided which responses run automatically and which require approval. When a SHA-256 hash from an Elastic Defend alert becomes the seed for a cross-mailbox quarantine, the artifact to preserve is the chain of evidence linking the endpoint event to the original email telemetry record. That linkage is what justifies the blast-radius action and what an IR review will need. Full integration documentation and workflow guidance are in the report.

item.title: Storm-3168, Linked to JADEPUFFER, Abused Stolen Azure Identities
item.description:
Storm-3168, tracked by Sysdig as JADEPUFFER, used two stolen Azure service principals to destroy over 100 storage accounts in seven minutes and harvest keys, in what Sysdig called the first documented agentic ransomware operation.
Key findings:
- The initial access vector is the headline forensic lesson. Credentials (client ID, client secret, and tenant ID) for one of the compromised service principals were posted in plaintext in a public GitHub issue by an employee of the victim organization. The issue was later edited to remove the secret, but GitHub preserves the full edit history, leaving the credentials accessible. Microsoft explicitly could not confirm this was the route used, but the warning is unambiguous: removing a post does not invalidate the credential. Defenders should treat any secret visible in public edit history as fully compromised and requiring immediate revocation, not just redaction.
- The attack split work across two service principals from the same tenant to separate reconnaissance from destruction. The first identity spent 15 hours 30 minutes completing more than 300 read operations. Ninety minutes later, the second enumerated the same environment across two subscriptions in five seconds. Both used the same Storm-3168 infrastructure, the same network fingerprint, and the user agent python-requests/2.34.2, a consistent behavioral signature across the operation. Overlapping token streams and precise inter-operation timing point to fully scripted or automated execution.
- The destructive phase lasted approximately seven minutes inside a 35-minute window of more than 150 destructive and credential-related operations. The second identity attempted deletion of over 100 storage accounts, a Key Vault, a Function App, and an App Service plan. It also targeted Azure Site Recovery and Azure Backup protection locks, and prioritized storage accounts with names referencing Terraform and backups, signaling deliberate recovery interference. Azure resource locks and deletion protection stopped several deletions, demonstrating that independent controls survive even broad Contributor-level compromise.
- Thirty minutes after the last deletion, the identity returned for keys. More than 30 successful ListKeys requests followed, including against Azure Site Recovery-linked accounts. One storage account in the same resource group as the deleted Key Vault was deliberately spared during destruction, then hit with a successful key request afterward, suggesting staged data theft preparation rather than pure destruction.
- The three IP addresses linked to Storm-3168 probing and malicious requests are 45.131.66[.]106, 34.153.223[.]102, and 64.20.53[.]230. Separate scanning from the same infrastructure targeted Azure App Services across different customers, hitting WordPress admin paths, PHP-CGI, and the LangFlow code validation endpoint at /api/v1/validate/code. None of those probes reached the affected subscriptions.
Hunt your Azure Activity Logs for ListKeys operations on storage accounts following resource deletion events, especially within the same resource group and within 30 minutes of destructive activity. Flag any service principal using python-requests/2.34.2 making bulk read operations. Audit service principal permissions for overly broad Storage Account Contributor or Contributor roles and cross-reference against GitHub, public issue trackers, and repository histories for exposed client secrets. Full IOC details and Microsoft's defensive guidance are in the report.

item.title: ShinyHunters Breached the FBI by Bypassing the Fix by Lucie Cardiet
item.description:
ShinyHunters breached the FBI's jobs portal via an unpatched Oracle PeopleSoft flaw, bypassing a published firewall workaround to steal agent PII and pivot into AWS government cloud storage.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-35273 is the Oracle PeopleSoft vulnerability at the center of this. Oracle patched it June 10, 2026, following Mandiant's report of zero-day exploitation against universities. Organizations that only applied the recommended firewall rule as a temporary control were not protected: by September, ShinyHunters had identified a single-character substitution in the web request that caused the firewall rule to miss the attack entirely while PeopleSoft processed it normally. The patch closed the hole; the workaround did not.
- The attack chain here is meaningfully different from ShinyHunters' prior campaigns. Earlier operations, including the Anodot/Snowflake wave and related helpdesk social engineering runs, relied on stolen credentials, token theft from SaaS integration providers, or MFA reset abuse. The login succeeded and looked legitimate. The FBI breach required no password at all: exploitation of a publicly accessible web application established a foothold directly on the server, then pivoted into FBI-managed Amazon government cloud storage. If your detection logic is tuned for post-authentication anomalies, you are watching the wrong layer for this intrusion class.
- Mandiant tracks this activity as UNC6240. ShinyHunters is the name on the leak site. Those are not interchangeable designations, and conflating them obscures which operators ran which campaigns and through which infrastructure. The report notes that when Scattered Spider, Lapsus$, and ShinyHunters announced they were going dark last September, the techniques and infrastructure did not follow. Operator branding changes; access methods persist.
- Scope of the September wave is broader than the FBI headline. Mandiant observed compromised PeopleSoft systems across higher education, technology, healthcare, agriculture, transportation, and government organizations globally. The FBI case has press; the others are being worked through quietly. ShinyHunters claims 2 to 3 terabytes exfiltrated from the FBI portal and downstream storage. The FBI has confirmed only that it is investigating.
- The group's stated motivation breaks from their pattern. Rather than a financial ransom, they published a PSA on their dark web leak site demanding the FBI retract or remove a May 2026 advisory that attributed harassment, swatting, and sextortion tactics to them. The deadline was September 30. The advisory remains up as of publication. Using stolen government personnel data as leverage against law enforcement's own public documentation is a different threat model than a standard pay-or-leak demand, and it changes what escalation looks like in the response timeline.
Practitioner takeaway: If you run Oracle PeopleSoft, the only confirmed protection is the patch for CVE-2026-35273 released June 10. Firewall-only mitigations are bypass-able as of September and should not be treated as closed controls. On already-exposed systems, Mandiant's follow-up report published September 25 covers what to look for on potentially compromised hosts. For hunting, the pivot from a PeopleSoft web tier into cloud-hosted storage is your lateral movement signal: look for outbound connections and data staging activity originating from the PeopleSoft application server process, not from an identity event. Full remediation guidance is in the Mandiant report.

item.title: Oh Look, The Foot Gun Went Off Again (Citrix NetScaler PreAuth Command Injection CVE-2026-88771)
item.description:
CVE-2026-88771: Pre-auth command injection in Citrix NetScaler Gateway gives unauthenticated attackers root on the appliance, exploited as a zero-day before any patch existed. Part of an eight-CVE bulletin including a second zero-day (CVE-2026-88772).
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-88771 carries a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.5 Critical and was actively exploited in the wild before Citrix issued a fix. The root cause is in ns_monuploadd_err.pl, a Perl script that historically parsed Pitboss crash logs using a backtick shell pipeline (grep | sed | awk). Attacker-controlled text passed via the login field of POST /nf/auth/doAuthentication.do gets written to NetScaler logs verbatim, then later consumed by that script. Because the old code interpolated the unsanitized log value directly into a second backtick command executing find, semicolons in the attacker's input were treated as shell command separators, executing arbitrary code as root. The second zero-day, CVE-2026-88772 (CVSS 9.5), is a DTLS memory overflow affecting VPN virtual servers enabled by default.
- The injection path is broad. Watchtowr's report confirms the vulnerable log sink is not limited to the authentication endpoint: failed logins, rate-limited requests, User-Agent headers, and other HTTP fields that land in logs can all carry the payload. The Citrix management interface is also in scope. A single unauthenticated POST with a crafted login parameter like "pitboss PPE unexpectedly died NSPPE;:id>/var/tmp/watchTowr;# X" is sufficient to plant the payload in the log. Execution happens when ns_monuploadd_err.pl runs, which can take up to 24 hours under normal scheduling, though Watchtowr notes a technique to force immediate execution exists and is being withheld.
- For forensic examination, look for suspicious entries in NetScaler's SSLVPN and AAATM log streams referencing "AAAD API: sending login req" or "process_kernel_socket: call to authenticate user" where the username field contains shell metacharacters (semicolons, backticks, pipes, redirection operators). The log format timestamps these with GMT and PPE identifier (e.g. 0-PPE-0). Any unexpected files in /var/tmp or /tmp, especially those owned by root and created in that timeframe, should be treated as command execution artifacts. Check /var/log and syslog-forwarded equivalents for the log entries shown in the report.
- The fixed versions are NetScaler ADC and Gateway 14.1-73.37, 13.1-64.23, 14.1-FIPS 14.1-73.37, and 13.1-FIPS/NDcPP 13.1-37.279. The fix replaces the shell pipeline with safe Perl file I/O and a strict regex that captures only (NSPPE-\d{2}) and (\d+) from log lines, then passes find arguments as a list rather than a shell string, eliminating interpolation entirely. CVE-2026-88778 (CVSS 8.8) requires an additional step beyond patching: Enhanced ISN Generation must be explicitly enabled.
Hunt priority: search NetScaler logs for login-field values containing semicolons, backticks, or redirection characters in SSLVPN Message and AAATM Message entries. Correlate creation timestamps of unexpected files under /var/tmp and /tmp against those log events. Given that exploitation predates the patch and Watchtowr describes APT-level interest, treat any unpatched appliance exposed to the internet as potentially already compromised and consider forensic imaging before upgrading.

item.title: 16,415 Stolen Passwords, One Open Door: How Blackhatsect0r & DXQRTXX Exposed Themselves
item.description:
A threat actor crew exposed their own live operational server through the same HTTP misconfiguration they had mocked victims for, handing researchers a full view of 16,415 stolen credentials, custom C2 source code, and months of internal chat logs.
Key findings:
- ThreatMon discovered a publicly reachable server belonging to the Blackhatsect0r / DXQRTXX crew, active May to August 2026, left open via unauthenticated directory listing. The exposure handed researchers the complete workshop: GHOST C2 v6.0, a roughly 13,000-line Go-based command-and-control framework with modules for scanning, credential extraction, exploitation, and reverse-shell handling, alongside a 17,826-line Python Discovery Engine that queries Certificate Transparency logs and brute-forces subdomains every two minutes against a queue built to hold over one million targets. SQLite databases held 16,415 credential records covering database dumps, SMTP accounts, AWS access keys, GitHub tokens, and API keys, plus a target list of roughly 498,000 URLs including 449 French 🇫🇷 government subdomains.
- Two targeted operations showed sustained manual tradecraft layered on top of automated scanning. Against ANTAI, France 🇫🇷's traffic-fine payment portal, the crew reverse-engineered the Angular JavaScript bundle and pulled three hardcoded cryptographic constants: an AES IV, a PBKDF2 salt, and a passphrase (troiscitronbosechatjouerbelierlawingssourisfermentpoids), then used ghost_token_forger.py to mint valid authentication tokens without credentials. They followed up with JWT algorithm confusion testing (none, HS256, HS384), HTTP request smuggling against an F5 BIG-IP at 90.102.74[.]9, and WAF bypass via X-HTTP-Method-Override headers against the Worldline perimeter.
- Against Coinstable.io, GHOST C2 found an exposed .env file containing a JWT signing secret literally set to the string "secret". The script coinstable_admin.py forged an administrator token with is_admin, can_withdraw, and 2fa_verified all set to true, then enumerated the full user list via admin API a thousand accounts at a time. coinstable_drain.py queried BTC, LTC, USDT, ETH, DOGE, and MATIC balances directly against the backend at 212.27.13[.]112 and staged withdrawals to attacker-controlled wallets, with a third script attempting weak confirmation codes (000000, 123456, 111111) before hunting undocumented endpoints.
- The crew operated a public Telegram channel (649 subscribers) under the identity DXQ SQUAD, including associated handles ElPr0fessor999, KushSEC, and Whitwhy Dx. The channel evolved from database leak announcements to distributing offensive tooling, including a 62MB Cobalt Strike package, with a follower poll in August choosing tools over stolen data by a clear margin. On July 28 DXQRTXX posted an OPSEC warning to the channel; the server containing their credential vault and source code was open the entire time.
DFIR takeaway: the two exploitation chains here leave examinable artifacts defenders can hunt for now. Frontend JavaScript bundles shipping cryptographic constants or passphrases are scanner-visible from the outside; internally, check application deployments for secrets committed to client-side code using static analysis against build artifacts. For the .env exposure pattern, review web server access logs for requests to /.env, /.env.local, and similar paths, these show as GET 200 responses and are a strong indicator of active reconnaissance or exfiltration. JWT abuse leaves a fingerprint in application logs: look for tokens with alg:none or unexpected algorithm values, and admin-scoped claims appearing on accounts that never completed normal auth flows. item.description:

Key details:
- CVE-2026-88771 is an improper input validation flaw (CWE-20) enabling unauthenticated remote command execution on any affected NetScaler ADC or Gateway build, no special configuration required. CVE-2026-88772 is a memory overflow (CWE-119, CWE classification) that enables RCE or DoS when DTLS is enabled, and Citrix notes DTLS is on by default for VPN virtual servers. Both carry CVSS v4.0 scores of 9.5 and were exploited before public patches existed. No public PoC has been independently verified, but real-world exploitation is confirmed by Citrix and CISA. No attribution to a specific actor has been established.
- Fixed builds per Citrix CTX697096: NetScaler ADC/Gateway 14.1 needs 14.1-73.37 or later; 13.1 needs 13.1-64.23 or later; 14.1-FIPS needs 14.1-73.37 FIPS or later; 13.1-FIPS/NDcPP needs 13.1-37.279 or later. A recent patch cycle does not guarantee protection; the exact running build must be verified. Secure Private Access Hybrid deployments using customer-managed NetScaler instances are also in scope. Citrix-managed cloud services are handled by Cloud Software Group.
- The DFIR posture shift here is critical: patching closes the hole but does not answer whether the appliance was already compromised during the zero-day window. CISA explicitly warns that applying updates can reduce forensic visibility. The Dutch 🇳🇱 NCSC has advised preserving logging and memory evidence before remediation on exposed systems. For suspected-compromised appliances, Citrix's own guidance recommends generating a Packet Engine core file before upgrading (note: triggers a warm restart).
- Evidence to preserve before disruptive changes includes: local and remotely forwarded NetScaler syslog, NetScaler Console data, SIEM and perimeter telemetry, VPN and authentication logs, appliance configuration, VM snapshots for VPX deployments, technical support bundles, and network connections to systems behind the appliance. Document system time, timezone, and NTP settings before isolation. NetScaler Console's File Integrity Monitoring can flag modified or newly added files, though Citrix cautions it does not catch every technique.
- Citrix has made IOCs available through NetScaler Console's IoC detection feature, which can run compromise-detection scans against managed appliances. Citrix explicitly warns these IOCs do not cover every TTP or attacker infrastructure component. A clean scan is not proof of no compromise. Organizations with reasonable suspicion of compromise should pursue broader forensic investigation beyond a single indicator scan.
Practitioner takeaway: Do not treat this as patch-and-close. Inventory every customer-managed NetScaler ADC and Gateway instance, verify the exact running build against CTX697096, and determine whether the appliance was internet-facing while vulnerable. If it was, run a compromise assessment: pull NetScaler Console IOC scans, review File Integrity Monitoring output, examine authentication and VPN logs for anomalous sessions, and check outbound connections from the appliance to unexpected destinations. Where compromise is suspected, preserve the Packet Engine core file and VM snapshot first, then isolate, revoke exposed credentials and secrets, and rebuild from known-good state. Disabling DTLS reduces the CVE-2026-88772 attack surface but leaves CVE-2026-88771 fully exploitable. IOCs are available via NetScaler Console for managed appliances.

item.title: Introducing ADE-Skills — Adversarial Detection Engineering Knowledge Base
item.description:
ADE-Skills launches as a public knowledge base for adversarial detection engineering, cataloging 37 technique files and nearly 600 candidate bypass findings across Elastic, Microsoft Sentinel, and Sigma rulesets.
Key details:
- The core of the repo is a four-category taxonomy of detection-logic failure modes: ADE1 covers reformatting in actions (NTFS 8.3 short names, PowerShell tick-escaping, environment-variable splicing), ADE2 covers omitted equivalence-class members (certutil -verifyctl/-decode/-URL while only -urlcache is watched, pwsh.exe while only powershell.exe is listed), ADE3 covers context manipulation (process-name cloning, activity spreading across entities, correlation-window timing, parent-process spoofing), and ADE4 covers Boolean and field-logic errors including negated filters that reference fields absent from a customer's telemetry, which can silently swallow true positives or disable themselves depending on how the backend evaluates a missing field.
- Each of the 37 technique files follows a fixed structure: summary, ADE classification, the technique, a vulnerable rule, a hardened rule, detection layers that survive the bypass, implementation nuances, and references. A good number are anchored to named vendor rules, giving practitioners a direct line from the abstract gap to a concrete rule they may already be running.
- Platform-specific bug-pattern catalogs cover Elastic Security, Microsoft Sentinel, and Sigma. Highlighted assumptions that quietly fail include Windows 4688 command-line auditing being off by default and script block logging disappearing after a PowerShell v2 downgrade, both of which can make a rule receive no data at all rather than fire incorrectly.
- The findings catalog contains 593 candidate bypass findings machine-extracted from public rulesets and mapped to the taxonomy with affected fields, the gap, and a suggested fix. The false-negative checklist provides four lenses: does the rule receive the data it needs, does it hinge on a threshold a slower technique avoids, does it cover only one binary or version when others are in scope, and is it tuned against a baseline that does not match the environment.
Practitioner takeaway: pull a rule you own, identify every member of its equivalence class (LOLBin aliases, alternate flags, short-name paths), confirm the required telemetry is actually enabled on the hosts that matter, and check any negated filters against fields your SIEM actually populates. item.title: The Infostealer Incursion: How Stolen Credentials Breach Cloud, Code, and AI Environments
item.description:
Infostealers targeting developer endpoints are the primary on-ramp to cloud, code, and AI environments. Lumma, RedLine, and Vidar account for 85.7% of detected incidents, and AWS credentials alone represent 46% of all compromised secrets harvested from infected machines.
Key findings:
- The infostealer supply chain is industrialized. Lumma C2, RedLine, and Vidar dominate MaaS platforms renting for a few hundred dollars a month. Stolen logs flow through Initial Access Brokers who validate credentials before selling verified access to ransomware operators. The window from a developer's phishing click to a live credential listing can be hours. Beyond passwords, NordStellar identified over 400 distinct non-credential secret types being harvested, including API keys, OAuth tokens, PATs, and active session cookies. GitHub credentials appear in roughly 50% of all infostealer families analyzed, ranking it the fourth most targeted secret type overall. AI platforms represent 5% of stolen secrets, led by OpenAI API keys, with Claude Code credentials now appearing in post-exploitation tooling like PEASS-ng (linPEAS/winPEAS) via sensitive_files.yaml.
- The file paths targeted are hardcoded and predictable, which cuts both ways for defenders. On AWS: ~/.aws/credentials (long-term IAM Access Key ID and Secret Access Key), ~/.aws/sso/cache/ (OIDC tokens lasting up to 90 days, continuously mintable into fresh STS credentials), and ~/.aws/cli/cache/ (short-lived STS tokens, 1-12 hours). On Azure: %USERPROFILE%\.azure\accessTokens.json (raw plaintext access tokens and long-lived refresh tokens), %USERPROFILE%\.azure\msal_token_cache.* (MSAL session data), and %localappdata%\.IdentityService\msal.cache or msalv2.cache (Entra ID tokens with Application Client IDs enabling app impersonation). Vidar 2.0 specifically enumerates %USERPROFILE%\.azuredirectory for Azure credential extraction. On GCP: ~/.config/gcloud/credentials.db and access_tokens.db (SQLite databases with OAuth 2.0 refresh tokens that do not auto-expire), and application_default_credentials.json. The TeamPCP LiteLLM supply chain infostealer had these exact GCP paths hardcoded.
- Session token theft is the preferred MFA bypass, and browser stores are the primary collection point. Infostealers extract cookies from on-disk browser caches or directly from browser process memory via code injection or debug API attachment. For GitHub, the cookies user_session, __Host-user_session_same_site, and _gh_sess grant full account access and bypass MFA entirely. For GitLab, the _gitlab_session cookie serves the same purpose. ChatGPT sessions are hijacked via the __Secure-next-auth.session-token cookie, exposing chat history that frequently contains proprietary code and internal business data. Ghost Loader specifically pulls ~/.ssh/id_rsa for long-term GitHub access. GitLab Runner config.toml files (containing glrt- prefixed tokens) let attackers register rogue CI/CD runners and intercept pipeline secrets. For Claude Code on Linux, ~/.claude/.credentials.json (mode 0600) stores portable OAuth refresh tokens: copying that file to another machine grants immediate access and the ability to invoke configured MCP servers.
- CI/CD pipelines are now a direct infostealer target without phishing. Miasma-style malware compromises software dependencies and hijacks build processes, targeting CI tokens, cloud credentials, and deployment artifacts directly in pipeline execution environments rather than on developer workstations. CVE-2023-7028 in self-hosted GitLab instances was exploited to distribute StealC via the Amadey loader, harvesting browser credentials and session cookies at scale.
- DFIR takeaway: When responding to a suspected infostealer incident on a developer endpoint, your first priority is revoking the long-lived tokens before hunting the malware. The AWS SSO OIDC tokens in ~/.aws/sso/cache/ and GCP OAuth refresh tokens in credentials.db can remain valid for 90 days or indefinitely unless explicitly revoked. Start there, then pull accessTokens.json and the MSAL caches on Azure. For GitHub and GitLab, check for rogue runners registered after the infection window and audit CI/CD variable access logs. Hunt browser process memory access anomalies (child processes or unexpected processes calling browser debug APIs) and scan for vbc.exe abuse or trojanized executables (Roblox.exe, ValorantSkinChanger.exe) as execution lures. The full file path appendix for all targeted secrets across AWS, Azure, GCP, GitHub, GitLab, OpenAI, and Claude Code is in the Wiz report.

item.title: ShinyHunters Renewed Mass Exploitation Campaign Targeting Oracle PeopleSoft
item.description:
ShinyHunters (UNC6240)-targeting group bypasses WAF mitigations to resume mass exploitation of CVE-2026-35273 in Oracle PeopleSoft, deploying web shells and a signed backdoor across dozens of systems globally in higher education, healthcare, government, and more.
- CVE-2026-35273 was first exploited as a zero-day in May-June 2026, primarily against universities. Oracle patched it June 10. UNC6240 returned in this wave targeting organizations that blocked /PSEMHUB/ at the WAF but never patched: they simply re-encoded the path as /%50SEMHUB/ (where %50 decodes to "P"). WAF and reverse proxy rules matching the literal string before URL normalization never fire. WebLogic decodes it and routes the request normally. This is a textbook WAF bypass, and it worked at scale because defenders trusted their perimeter rule as a compensating control.
- The attack chain is methodical. Before full exploitation, servers receive 5-15 POST requests to /%50SEMHUB/hub carrying a serialized Java object that confirms exploitability without writing files, a quiet fingerprint step responders will find only in WebLogic access logs. Exploitation then follows one of two paths: JSP web shell drop into PSEMHUB.war (x.jsp for command execution, u.jsp/u2.jsp for chunked file upload), or fileless command execution where output returns directly in the HTTP response and no JSP is written at all. Detections keyed only on new JSP file creation will miss the fileless path entirely. On load-balanced environments, the actor sent burst POST requests to seed every node behind the balancer.
- On compromised Windows hosts, UNC6240 uploaded Ple64.exe (tracked as SIDEEYE), a 5.2 MB trojanized Light Alloy media player installer signed with a valid EV certificate issued to Tobias Weihmann Software Development OU via Sectigo. It runs a three-stage in-memory chain: Stage 1 decompresses a VMProtect 3-protected launcher, which decrypts and loads Stage 3, the SIDEEYE C++ backdoor. SIDEEYE calls home to 162.219.30[.]165 over raw TCP on ports 3333 (control) and 3334 (data) and supports credential theft, file and process management, and reverse shell/proxy. Neo-reGeorg tunnel.jsp and tunnel.jspx were staged alongside for SOCKS5 tunneling through HTTP/HTTPS. On Linux, MeshAgent was dropped to /tmp (meshagent, meshagent.msh, meshagent.db) under the PeopleSoft service account; September 2026 intrusions pivoted to winmanage-me[.]network on 104.219.234[.]138.
- Scope and impact are serious. A quarter of observed post-exploitation commands ran as root or NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM. The rest ran as PeopleSoft or WebLogic service accounts, still enough to reach database connection strings, HR and payroll tables, and student records. UNC6240 has an established extortion pattern: steal data, threaten public release. Affected sectors include higher education, healthcare, government, technology, agriculture, and transportation globally.
Practitioner takeaway: If you blocked /PSEMHUB/ at the WAF and considered it mitigated, assume that control has failed and treat unpatched hosts as potentially compromised. Hunt WebLogic access logs for /%50SEMHUB/ and all percent-encoded or mixed-case variants of that path, enforce blocking on the URL-normalized form. Scan PSEMHUB.war/ and PORTAL.war/ for x.jsp, u.jsp, u2.jsp, tunnel.jsp, tunnel.jspx, and Ple64.exe. Alert on cmd.exe or /bin/sh spawned by the WebLogic Java process, especially invoking base64 -d, tasklist, start /b, or curl. Check /tmp for meshagent binaries and review outbound TCP to ports 3333/3334 and rsync (TCP 873). Rotate all credentials reachable from the PeopleSoft tier. Google Security Operations customers: detection rules including "Oracle PeopleSoft Suspicious File Write to Web Application Archive Directory" are available or pending in the Mandiant Frontline Threats rule pack. item.title: Threat Actors Use Google Ads To Target Ledger Users
item.description:
Crypto wallet phishing campaign abuses Google Ads, Cloud Storage, Vercel, and Google Sites in a layered redirect chain to steal Ledger recovery phrases from US 🇺🇸, European, and Asian users.
Key findings:
- The attack chain ran entirely through trusted platforms to bypass reputation-based filtering. A malicious sponsored Google ad, placed under a compromised verified advertiser account (listed with a Germany 🇩🇪 location), sent victims to a Google Cloud Storage URL, which redirected to a Vercel-hosted page, which then loaded a Google Sites page displaying the phishing content inside an iframe. Every hop used infrastructure with inherent trust signals that made blocking by domain reputation alone unreliable.
- The Vercel redirect domain rotated approximately every 15-20 minutes during analysis, meaning any IOC-based block on a specific Vercel subdomain would have a short effective window. Two captured HTML samples confirmed the JavaScript redirect pointed to different Vercel-hosted domains across that interval. The attacker could update the delivery chain while the Google Cloud Storage page remained static and unchanged.
- The phishing page impersonated Ledger's interface with download options for Windows, macOS, Linux, and mobile. It tracked device metadata and monitored keypresses, touches, and mouse movements, sending behavioral data to a Vercel-hosted endpoint, likely to distinguish real victims from automated sandboxes. A Cloudflare Web Analytics beacon was also embedded with an analytics token, giving the attacker passive visibility into visitor behavior.
- Recovery phrase collection used BIP-39 autocomplete pulled from api/bip39-english.txt to help users correctly type their 12-24 word seed. On first submission the phrase was sent to the attacker-controlled Vercel endpoint. The page then returned a fake "Invalid seed" error to prompt a second submission, which was also exfiltrated. An invisible hCaptcha widget was initialized during submission. No server-side comparison of the two entries was observed, confirming the double-submission was purely a collection mechanism.
- IOCs from the report include Google Cloud Storage bucket URLs: storage.googleapis[.]com/apf-leg-ad-23798/, storage.googleapis[.]com/ledg-leg1-79230/, storage.googleapis[.]com/apf-leg-ad-22076/, and storage.googleapis[.]com/apf-leg-ad-32595/. Google Sites URLs: sites.google[.]com/view/start-ledger-wallet, sites.google[.]com/view/apps-ledger-wallet, and sites.google[.]com/view/download-ledger-wallet-pc. Vercel domains include soyyoo-cwpc5n0e.vercel[.]app, rpc-gbz5.vercel[.]app, whyavc-qwmv6stx.vercel[.]app, router-wdoi.vercel[.]app, and node-f1ey.vercel[.]app.

Hunt proxy and DNS logs for the GCS bucket paths and Google Sites URLs above, and alert on iframe loads sourced from sites.google[.]com pointing outbound to vercel[.]app subdomains. For broader coverage, flag any page embedding an iframe that loads cross-origin content from a Vercel subdomain alongside a BIP-39 wordlist fetch, an invisible hCaptcha initialization, or behavioral telemetry POSTs. item.title: From Debugging to Code Execution: RCE in Microsoft DevLabs’ DebugMCP?
item.description:
Drive-by RCE in Microsoft DevLabs' DebugMCP v1.1.4 lets a malicious webpage execute arbitrary code on a developer's machine via DNS rebinding and a UNC path file execution primitive, no user interaction beyond visiting a page.
Technical breakdown:
- DebugMCP installs from the VS Code Marketplace with one click and immediately starts an unauthenticated JSON-RPC MCP server on port 3001, listening without host or origin validation. The custom Express configuration skips the createMcpExpressApp middleware introduced in modelcontextprotocol SDK v1.23.0, which would have added validateHostHeader and validateOriginHeader by default. That omission is the core of the DNS rebinding exposure, also referenced as related to CVE-2025-53967 in structure.
- The transport was configured in stateless mode: sessionIdGenerator set to undefined causes validateSession to return immediately, bypassing the initialize handshake entirely. A single no-cors HTTP POST to /mcp?transport=streamable_http is enough to invoke any tool, no prior session establishment required.
- The start_debugging tool accepts a fileFullPath argument with no sanitization. On Windows, UNC paths of the form \\ATTACKER\SHARE\payload.py are passed straight through to VS Code's debugging infrastructure and then to the Python launcher, which reaches out to the attacker's SMB share, fetches the script, and executes it under the victim's user context.
- The full attack chain: victim visits attacker page, DNS TTL expires (1-2 seconds), rebind resolves attacker domain to 127.0.0.1, browser considers the subsequent fetch to evil.attacker[.]com:3001 same-origin, request hits local DebugMCP, Python launcher pulls payload from attacker SMB share, code runs. Firefox versions before 153 and browsers lacking Local Network Access protections do not block this. The fix shipped silently in commit 86776b2 with no advisory or CVE issued; v1.2.0 contains the patch.
- Impact is severe because the target is a developer workstation: live AWS keys, SSH keys, GitHub tokens, active cloud CLI sessions, VPN tunnels, and push access to production branches are all inherited by the payload silently. This is a realistic supply-chain pivot path: compromising a developer machine is often a shorter route to production than attacking production directly.
Practitioners responding to a potential exploitation event should examine VS Code extension logs and the DebugMCP server output on port 3001 for unexpected JSON-RPC tool calls, particularly start_debugging invocations with UNC paths. On Windows, look for outbound SMB (port 445) connections originating from the VS Code Python launcher process at the time of the suspected visit. Browser history and DNS cache artifacts can help correlate the rebind timing. For hunting across a developer fleet, query for processes where the VS Code debugger process spawned unexpected child processes or made outbound network connections to external IPs. Developers still on v1.1.4 must update to v1.2.0 or later. Audit all listening loopback ports on developer machines and enforce authentication on any MCP server in your environment. item.title: Master Key Included: Detecting SolarWinds ARM CVE-2026-28326
item.description:
CVE-2026-28326 is an unauthenticated RCE in SolarWinds Access Rights Manager, CVSS 8.8 (adjacent) to 9.8 (flat network), confirmed NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM execution, patched in build 2026.2.1.7.
- The root cause is a hardcoded shared HMAC secret shipped in the installer, identical across every deployment. ARM's gRPC listener on TCP 55555 accepts a fallback authentication path: present no client certificate, compute an HMAC token from the static key over attacker-controlled request fields, and the gate passes. The key is recoverable by anyone who can download the product. No nonce, no challenge, no binding to the channel. A valid token is mintable offline without touching the server.
- TLS on port 55555 does not close this. ARM configures the listener to request a client certificate and verify it if presented, but not to require one. A caller presenting nothing completes the TLS handshake anonymously, lands unauthenticated, and faces only the application-layer HMAC check as the sole control. The difference between "request" and "require" is one enum value in the configuration call. Any service described as mutual-TLS protected warrants the same verification.
- Past the gate, the connection reaches a BinaryFormatter deserialization sink carrying .NET Remoting traffic. The only protection was a denylist of 27 regex patterns over known gadget type names, applied to an unbounded type space. Bishop Fox built a working exploit chain against an unpatched lab server and confirmed command execution as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM via an out-of-band HTTP callback and a dropped file. Builds 2026.2.0.42 and earlier are affected.
- The firewall posture governs real-world CVSS. ARM's Windows Firewall rule for 55555 ships disabled and scoped to 127.0.0.1, but SolarWinds' own prerequisites instruct administrators to open it inbound so collectors can reach the server. On any working multi-host deployment the port is open. ARM console operators (ordinary admin workstations) are inside that allowlist. A flat or permissive internal network elevates the effective score to 9.8 AV:N. Read the actual firewall rule; do not inherit the vendor's adjacency assumption.
- Before patching, look for evidence of prior use. The GrantMA service exposes GET /api/armconfig/network/Connections: a record showing IsAuthenticated: false paired with a populated ClientCertThumbPrint is the signature the vulnerable fallback path produces and a legitimate client login does not. This list is memory-only and purges entries after three days, so query it before the service restart that applies the patch wipes it. The patch rewrites the gate entirely, replacing the HMAC fallback with a localhost-only check tied to a per-process random GUID, so patching removes the path rather than hardening it.
Takeaway: patch to 2026.2.1.7, query the connection list now before you restart the service, then read the actual firewall rule governing 55555 and treat a permissive rule as a separate exposure finding. Bishop Fox's detection tool (available on GitHub as CVE-2026-28326-check) fingerprints patch state from outside using two anonymous gRPC probes: a vulnerable build returns gRPC status 14 UNAVAILABLE on the Remoting/Send call, while a patched build returns gRPC status 16 UNAUTHENTICATED with the message "Client certificate not found. Please register your application first." An inconclusive result is not a clean one.

item.title: Storm-3168: Agentic-driven cloud attacks using compromised service principals
item.description:
Storm-3168 (JADEPUFFER) used compromised Azure service principals to destroy storage, key vaults, and app resources in a 7-minute automated blitz, then pivoted to credential harvesting, marking the first detailed view of this agentic ransomware operator's Azure activity.
Key findings:
- Initial access likely came from a service principal's client ID, client secret, and tenant ID exposed in plaintext in a public GitHub issue. The employee later edited the issue to remove the secret, but GitHub's public edit history retained the credentials in full. This is the core forensic lesson: removing an exposed secret does not invalidate it. Revoke and rotate immediately, then audit the identity's full activity history from the date of first exposure forward.
- Two compromised service principals divided the work under a coordinated, automated playbook. The first ran reconnaissance for 15+ hours, executing 300+ read operations across VMs, subscriptions, and resource groups. The second began its own enumeration 90 minutes later, then pivoted to App Service config stores looking for additional credentials. Both shared the same network fingerprint and user agent string: python-requests/2.34.2. MITRE ATT&CK techniques T1078.004 (Valid Accounts: Cloud Accounts) and T1526 (Cloud Service Discovery) map to this phase.
- The destructive sequence ran for approximately 7 minutes and included 100+ Azure Storage account deletion attempts, plus Key Vault, Function App, and App Service plan deletions. SQL database deletions were attempted in parallel but failed due to an unsupported API version, an investigative artifact worth noting: failed ARM operations in logs can expose intended scope even when the action didn't land. Azure resource locks and storage-level deletion protection blocked a subset of storage deletions, demonstrating that independent safeguards hold even when the compromised identity holds broad administrative rights. T1485 (Data Destruction) and T1490 (Inhibit System Recovery) apply here.
- Approximately 30 minutes after the destructive phase, the same service principal issued 30+ successful ListKeys requests against Azure Storage Accounts via ARM, including Site Recovery-related accounts. Five unique OAuth tokens were observed for this identity, four scoped to deletion, one to inventory and key retrieval, with two deletion tokens active simultaneously during a 70-second window. This token segmentation is a strong indicator of scripted or agentic orchestration and is visible in Azure AD sign-in and ARM audit logs.
- IOCs from the report: 45.131.66[.]106 (App Service probing and malicious ARM requests), 34.153.223[.]102 (App Service probing), 64.20.53[.]230 (App Service probing). Storm-3168 linked infrastructure also probed WordPress admin paths, PHP-CGI endpoints, and LangFlow's /api/v1/validate/code endpoint across multiple Azure App Services throughout 2026.
Practitioner takeaway: Start your hunt in Azure Activity Logs and Entra audit logs. Look for service principals issuing bulk delete operations against Storage, Key Vault, or SQL resources in compressed time windows, especially where multiple tokens for the same identity overlap. Flag any ListKeys call following a destructive sequence as a likely credential-harvesting pivot. Check ARM logs for failed deletes: the unsupported API version error on SQL here revealed intended scope the attacker couldn't execute. Cross-reference all service principal activity back to public repos, issues, and CI/CD configs for plaintext credential exposure. item.title: ClickFix Campaign Abuses Trusted Websites to Deploy Psychedelic Stealer
item.description:
ClickFix campaign hijacks Ukrainian 🇺🇦 business websites to serve a fake Cloudflare CAPTCHA, deploying Psychedelic Stealer with persistent C2 tasking and crypto wallet harvesting across 32 countries.
- Six legitimate Ukrainian 🇺🇦 businesses, including a hair clinic, a bookseller, and an automotive retailer, had hidden iframes injected into their pages. Visitors who already trusted those sites were shown a convincing fake Cloudflare verification page, complete with a randomly generated hex "Ray ID" in the footer and a fixed "visitor identifier," both meaningless imitations of real Cloudflare markers. The page was written in Ukrainian 🇺🇦 but its HTML carried Russian-language comments and declared lang="ru", a construction detail worth noting for attribution context.
- The CAPTCHA click silently copies a msiexec.exe command to the clipboard and instructs the user to run it via Windows+R. No PowerShell is involved at this stage, a deliberate choice that bypasses detection controls focused on PowerShell execution. The downloaded MSI drops a 64-bit executable named psychedeliclove.exe. Psychedelic Stealer targets saved passwords from Chrome, Edge, Brave, Opera, Opera GX, Vivaldi, and Yandex, harvests browser account tokens, and goes after Exodus, Atomic Wallet, Electrum, Bitcoin Core, and Litecoin Core wallets.
- The implant is more than a one-shot stealer. It installs browser components, sets up a native messaging bridge for local process communication, creates a scheduled task named psychedelicloveUtils for persistence, profiles the host including antivirus status, and polls a C2 for follow-on tasks. Task state is tracked in executed_tasks.json and downloaded payloads land in downloads\taskid_filename. Supported payload types include EXE, COM, BAT, CMD, MSI, and PowerShell, meaning initial access is a foothold, not a finished operation.
- The campaign is managed through a panel called "РУБЛЁВКА TDS" (Rublevka TDS), named after the wealthy Rublevka district near Moscow. The panel centralizes payload URL control across all compromised sites without requiring per-page edits, and tracks CAPTCHA page opens, clicks, and Done-button events. At collection time it showed 557 views, 426 clicks, and 79 complete events across 32 countries, with Ukraine 🇺🇦 accounting for 446 views and 351 clicks. The infrastructure domain uasputnik[.]com was registered September 9, 2026, and lure URLs appeared within the same week.
- Network indicators to hunt: outbound traffic to uasputnik[.]com followed by a request to admin777111777.php signals early-stage delivery. Later-stage C2 traffic goes to 193.178.159[.]128:8080, specifically to /api/v1/agent/ and /api/v1/ext/ endpoints with an X-API-Key header. item.title: Dark Web Profile: Blue Locker Ransomware
item.description:
Blue Locker ransomware hit Pakistan 🇵🇰's second-largest oil and gas producer in August 2025, wiping backups and halting financial operations for two days. Attribution pulls toward Iranian-linked Proton family code, but the picture is deliberately murky.
- The August 6, 2025 attack on Pakistan 🇵🇰 Petroleum Limited encrypted servers and VMs, deleted shadow copies via wmic SHADOWCOPY DELETE (T1490), and stopped critical services (T1489) before triggering encryption. Operators claimed 1 TB exfiltrated. Pakistan 🇵🇰's NCERT issued an emergency advisory to 39 government ministries, including the Cabinet Division, FIA, FBR, and PEMRA. PPL denied sensitive data loss, but financial systems were down for two days at a company supplying roughly one-fifth of Pakistan 🇵🇰's natural gas.
- Attribution is genuinely unresolved. Resecurity links Blue Locker to the Proton ransomware family, sharing code with Shinra, Zola, Limba, and Cipher, all assessed with probable Iranian 🇮🇷 origins by Israel 🇮🇱's INCD and Fortinet's FortiGuard Labs. Separately, researcher rivitna classifies the same .blue / restore_file.txt artifacts as MemeCryptor, an open-source GitHub project by "DarkFunct" inspired by Conti, using ChaCha20+RSA with BMP steganography for key hiding. These threads are not mutually exclusive: Proton source has been sold on dark web forums and MemeCryptor is publicly available. The binary also contains Chinese-language strings including a reference to Qihoo 360's "ZhuDongFangYu" component, assessed as deliberate false flags, not evidence of Chinese 🇨🇳 origin.
- Name collision is a real contamination risk. Three distinct malware families share the .blue space: Blue Locker / MemeCryptor drops restore_file.txt and appends .blue. Proton / Shinra V2 also appends .blue but renames files to random 10-character strings and uses-files.txt or.txt. Phobos "Blue" is an entirely separate codebase. Validate against specific IOC sets before merging into a timeline or threat cluster.
- The attack chain uses a PowerShell loader for initial staging (NCERT mapped T1059.003), UAC bypass via registry manipulation (T1548.002), and persistence via registry Run keys under HKLMSOFTWAREMicrosoftWindowsNTCurrentVersionRun (T1547.001). The mutex string wbizecif48njqgpprzkm6769 prevents duplicate execution. Chrome.exe is forcibly terminated to unlock its credential database before encryption. Timestamps are manipulated (T1070.006) and sandbox checks (T1497) run before payload execution. Negotiation runs over ProtonMail hyebwma@protonmail[.]com, Jabber hsbwabwy@xmpp[.]jp, and a Tox ID, with no dedicated Tor leak site.
- Defanged IOCs from the NCERT advisory include domains shinra-encrypt-support[.]xyz, blue-decryptor[.]site, backup-leaks[.]fun, and locker-c2[.]onion, plus IPs including 185.225.69[.]140, 195.3.145[.]99, 91.243.113[.]21, and 103.150.199[.]23. SHA-256 hashes include d3cc6cc4538d57f2d1f8a9d46a3e8be73ed849f7fe37d1d969c0377cf1d0fadc and e6bd4ed287d1336206f5b4b65011e570267418799eb60c2d0d7496d5d9e95a33. Full IOC list including MD5 and SHA-1 from NCA-38 is in the report.
Hunt for the mutex wbizecif48njqgpprzkm6769, registry Run key writes under CurrentVersionRun paired with a randomly named binary in %Temp%, and chrome.exe termination followed immediately by file rename activity. The restore_file.txt ransom note and .blue extension are your on-disk confirmation, but timestomping means do not rely on file modification times for sequencing. Correlate against the NCERT NCA-38 IOC set before attributing to Proton or any other cluster.

item.title: Kothamine malware uses Tailscale’s tailcat to evade network detection
item.description:
Kothamine, a newly documented C/C++ RAT with 30+ commands, abuses Tailscale's tailcat tool to tunnel C2 traffic over WireGuard, stripping defenders of any conventional domain to block.
Key findings:
- Kothamine Injector drops itself to %ROAMING%\MicrosoftEdgeUpdateCore.exe and the agent DLL to %ROAMING%\MicrosoftEdgeUpdateCore.dll, then injects the DLL into explorer.exe via the classic OpenProcess/VirtualAllocEx/WriteProcessMemory/CreateRemoteThread/LoadLibraryA chain. Persistence lands via up.ps1 in %TEMP%, which registers a scheduled task named MicrosoftEdgeUpdateTask set to trigger at logon. The agent creates the mutex Local\KothamineAgentInstance on startup and immediately runs hidden PowerShell to add its own paths and processes to Windows Defender exclusions using Add-MpPreference.
- C2 runs entirely through tailcat.exe, extracted from the agent's resources and saved to %ROAMING%\TailscalePortable\tailcat.exe. The agent launches it with a forward flag and a tc-address, making operator infrastructure available on localhost:18080, then connects to 127.0.0.1:18080 and forwards to port 4444 on the operator's node. All traffic is encrypted with AES-GCM using a hardcoded base64 key. Because tailcat uses WireGuard's data plane with no accounts, no registered devices, and no control plane, there is no C2 domain or IP to pivot on from network logs alone.
- The plugin system is the capability multiplier. The load_feature command receives a base64-encoded DLL over C2, writes it to a temp path, loads it with LoadLibraryA, and calls a GetFeatureApi export that returns function pointers (init, exec, cleanup) stored in a global g_features map. Operators can hot-load arbitrary capabilities without touching disk beyond the temp DLL write. Separate builds already ship getdiscord, getsessions, screenshot, screenshare, and camera commands covering browser cookie theft, Steam and Minecraft session files, clipboard, screenshots, and live camera/microphone recording.
- The supply chain vector is malicious npm packages, including one named dotnet-runtime-base, which downloaded npm-sc-legit.exe (a compiled Kothamine build with stealer commands) from a GitHub repository at github[.]com/cphc811-ui/. The developer published compilation instructions for kothamine-stub-cpp inside one of the packages, an operational mistake that exposed the build pipeline. Two other packages by the same developer were removed. SHA-256 hashes for the injector (ec4219a7ecf132c29080fbb20e4ab410c57faa85aeed7acade1eb15d905a6ee0) and agent DLL (74eca3973ad72a6ddc9397aff8250d9ee287211fc9a055d5ee290d01cf76a70c) are in the report.
Hunt for the scheduled task MicrosoftEdgeUpdateTask and the mutex Local\KothamineAgentInstance first. Then look for explorer.exe loading an AppData\Roaming DLL and for tailcat.exe running as a child of any process with a forward argument containing a tc-address. On disk, check %ROAMING%\TailscalePortable\ and %ROAMING%\MicrosoftEdgeUpdateCore.*. Network-side, watch for WireGuard traffic (UDP) initiated by non-system processes and loopback connections to port 18080. Full IOC list is in the report.

item.title: AI-Powered CARBONATO Botnet Steals Credentials to Fund Its Own LLM Gateway
item.description:
AI-augmented botnet CARBONATO exploits unauthenticated Docker daemons to deploy an LLM-driven agent that steals AI API keys to fund the operators' own compute gateway, active since at least October 2024.
Key findings:
- Initial access is brutally simple: CARBONATO scans for Docker daemons listening unauthenticated on port 2375, then uses the Docker API itself to spin up a privileged container with the host filesystem mounted and runs commands directly on the underlying machine. entry.sh (versioned at 5.3) bootstraps the foothold by opening a reverse SSH tunnel to a relay in AS262145, a Costa Rican network, installing an SSH server, injecting the crew's own key, and firing a Telegram deployment report containing the container ID, hostname, IP, and country. The tunnel port is not random: it is derived from the MD5 hash of the victim's IP, letting operators recalculate the reconnect port without storing any state.
- Persistence is layered and hardened. Cron jobs, systemd timers, rc.local, and OpenRC entries are all written and then marked immutable so basic cleanup fails. The malicious container runs under the name "systemd-resolved," displays a fake systemd-networkd resolver banner, and masquerades its process arguments as a kernel thread named [kworker/u2:0]. A watchdog re-pulls the implant from the registry if the container disappears.
- The AI angle is what sets CARBONATO apart. The implant installs Hermes Agent, an MIT-licensed open-source framework from Nous Research, entirely unmodified. The only change is the persona file: /root/.hermes/SOUL.md is overwritten with a 39-line prompt that renames the agent "GH0ST" and directs it to execute tasks from Telegram, maintain persistence, and collect credentials. Operators send tasks via Telegram; the agent forwards them with the persona to an LLM gateway, which writes terminal commands, reads output, and decides next actions autonomously. The binary is clean; the malicious logic lives entirely in the prompt.
- Credential theft is explicitly prioritized. The SOUL.md prompt names 14 AI providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini, OpenRouter, Groq, Mistral, Cohere, and others) and ranks their API keys above SSH credentials, access tokens, and databases. The reason: the operators were running their own LLM gateway, observed live on September 3, serving 27 models through its API on a free tier funded entirely by stolen keys. The botnet's economy is self-sustaining: compromise hosts, steal AI credentials, use them to run the AI that runs the botnet.
- Attribution signals are convergent. Fourteen of 162 image configurations carry UTC-06:00 timestamps matching the America/Costa_Rica timezone. The Telegram operator handle is "Carbo506" and +506 is Costa Rica's country calling code. Tunnel infrastructure terminates in AS262145, a Costa Rican network. Deployment messages are written in voseo Spanish 🇪🇸. ThreatDown's researchers stumbled into the entire toolchain by finding the operators' own unauthenticated registry, which leaked 59 repositories, 234 tags, 605 verified file blobs, C2 addresses, bot tokens, and the shared password for the AI gateway in a single passive collection session.
Takeaway: Hunt for /root/.hermes/SOUL.md containing the string "GH0ST" and .env files carrying CARBONATO_API_KEY. Flag unexplained outbound Telegram traffic from server workloads. For container environments, audit for privileged containers with the host filesystem mounted and parent process Docker daemon spawning SSH servers. Rotate AI API keys stored anywhere on exposed infrastructure and monitor provider dashboards for unexpected usage spikes. The full IOC list and technical details are in the ThreatDown report.

item.title: Apple Biome Forensics: Artifacts, Locations, and SEGB format
item.description:
Apple Biome is now the primary pattern-of-life source on modern iPhones and iPads, replacing knowledgeC.db from iOS 14 onward. Understanding the SEGB binary format and where these files live is essential before any iOS investigation.
Key findings:
- Biome requires a full file system extraction, not an iTunes-style backup. Files live in two directories: /private/var/mobile/Library/Biome/ and /private/var/db/biome/. Inside each, a streams folder splits data into public and restricted subfolders. Notable streams include AppLaunch at /private/var/mobile/Library/Biome/streams/public/AppLaunch/, Safari history at /private/var/db/biome/streams/restricted/_DKEvent.Safari.History/, and app-in-focus at /private/var/db/biome/streams/restricted/_DKEvent.App.InFocus/. Each stream subdirectory typically holds a local folder for on-device records and a remote folder for data synced from other devices on the same Apple ID. Remote subfolders are named with the source device GUID, resolvable via sync.db at /private/var/mobile/Library/Biome/sync.db.
- Retention is approximately 28 days, controlled by a maxAge value of 2,419,200 seconds in a metadata plist inside each stream directory. Expired records may persist in a tombstone subfolder, potentially extending your timeline further back. Check the tombstone folder before concluding a stream has no older activity.
- Two SEGB versions exist and must be parsed differently. SEGB v1 covers iOS 15 and 16: the "SEGB" signature sits at offsets 52-55 of a 56-byte file header, and each record carries a 32-byte header containing payload length, a state flag (1 = written, 3 = deleted), two Mac Absolute Time timestamps, and a CRC32 checksum, with records aligned to 8-byte boundaries. SEGB v2 covers iOS 17 and later: the signature moves to offsets 0-3 of a 32-byte file header, the file is a fixed 1 MiB, and record metadata (state, end offset, creation timestamp) moves out of the record header and into 16-byte trailer entries indexed from the end of the file. Payload structure (Protobuf) is typically unchanged between versions for the same stream.
- Deleted records lose their payload. When a record is marked deleted (state = 3), the payload is overwritten with zeroed bytes. On iOS 18 SEGB v2 files, the entire record including the record header is zeroed. The trailer entry in v2 and the record header in v1 may still show that an event occurred at a given timestamp, even without recoverable content. Clearing all Safari browsing history caused SEGB payloads to be zeroed in testing, while deleting a single history item did not always immediately remove its record.
- The SEGB timestamps in v1 mark when the record was written, not necessarily when the event occurred. Build timelines carefully and corroborate Biome timestamps against other sources. For cross-device recovery, check the remote subfolder of any synced Apple device: a record deleted on one device may still be intact in the remote folder on another device sharing the same Apple ID.
Practitioner takeaway: On any iOS investigation from iOS 14 onward, pull both /private/var/mobile/Library/Biome/ and /private/var/db/biome/ as part of your full file system extraction workflow. Determine your iOS version first to know whether you are dealing with SEGB v1 (signature at offset 52) or v2 (signature at offset 0, fixed 1 MiB file). Check the tombstone folder for data beyond the 28-day active window, examine the remote folders for cross-device activity, and do not discard deleted records even when the payload is zeroed since the trailer or record header metadata can still anchor an event to a timestamp. knowledgeC.db remains present on iOS 18, so treat both sources as complementary, not redundant.

item.title: RemControl Banking Trojan Gives Attackers Remote Control of Android Devices
item.description:
Android banking trojan RemControl abuses Accessibility Services for full device takeover, targeting 30+ banking institutions across Western Europe, the Middle East, and Canada 🇨🇦 since July 2026.
Key findings:
- The dropper delivery chain is worth understanding in full. Victims are lured to fake Google Play Store pages impersonating the TVTap IPTV app, with pages dynamically localized via user-agent and IP geolocation. The dropper then launches a local VPN service to route Google Play Protect traffic through a null channel, effectively blinding Android's built-in malware scanner. It also generates a fresh signing key via the Android Keystore and uses it to sign the RemControl payload on the fly, defeating hash-based detection before installation even completes. VPN-based Play Protect suppression is being flagged by Group-IB as a recurring pattern in Android dropper development.
- Once installed, RemControl requests Accessibility Service permissions. If granted, the trojan achieves full device control: it inflates full-screen WebView overlays impersonating targeted banking apps to harvest PIN codes, mobile banking codes, and card expiry dates. It also performs real-time screen capture that returns a machine-readable map of every visible UI element including coordinates, text content, and interactive state, plus keylogging and pattern lock capture to track unlocks and input.
- The threat actor behind RemControl is tracked as UNKK, assessed as Russian-speaking. Notably, Group-IB assesses the developer used an AI assistant to build significant portions of the C2 backend and phishing overlays by framing credential-theft API endpoints as a parental monitoring application. The C2 panel API documentation was inadvertently exposed during analysis, giving researchers deep infrastructure visibility. The euphemistic language in the documentation, referring to banking victims as "a person staring at the quiz" and credential theft as "quiz completion," is a direct artifact of that AI-assisted development approach.
- C2 communications use a Telegram dead-drop to obscure the real server address, with the primary channel being a WebSocket using a JSON envelope with fields cmd, udid, rid, and data. RemControl also implements self-preservation: it actively blocks application removal and prevents access to factory reset screens, making victim-side remediation difficult without specialized tooling or ADB access.
Responder takeaway: On Android forensics engagements, look for unauthorized Accessibility Service grants in Settings logs and check the installed app signing certificate against the developer's claimed identity. A freshly generated Keystore signing key on a sideloaded APK is a hard indicator. Hunt for WebSocket connections to Telegram-adjacent infrastructure and inspect JSON traffic for the cmd/udid/rid/data envelope pattern. For threat hunters monitoring enterprise mobile fleets, flag any app invoking VPN APIs alongside Accessibility Service requests. The full technical breakdown and IOC detail are in the Group-IB report published September 23.
