item.title: Port Scanning vs Service Detection: What an Open Port Really Means
item.description:
Nightmare Eclipse: Abdelhamid Naceri's 2026 exploit stream targets Microsoft Defender, Windows recovery paths, and third-party endpoint agents across a chain of releases and remediation bypasses, with exploitation confirmed in the wild for two CVEs.
Key findings:
- The Nightmare Eclipse releases span local privilege escalation, protected-data access, recovery-path abuse, and endpoint-update disruption across Microsoft Defender, Kaspersky, CrowdStrike Falcon, Avast, and NVIDIA components. The core technique is consistent with Naceri's earlier Windows research: a trusted, high-privilege component processes files or state that a lower-privileged user can influence. CVEs confirmed in the Microsoft advisory data include CVE-2026-33825 (BlueHammer, platform first-fixed 4.18.26030.3011), CVE-2026-41091 (RedSun, engine 1.1.26040.8), CVE-2026-45498 (UnDefend, platform 4.18.26040.7), CVE-2026-50656 (RoguePlanet, engine 1.1.26060.3008), and CVE-2026-69414 (ShieldBreak, engine 1.1.26080.3). Microsoft marked exploitation as detected for RedSun and UnDefend.
- The remediation chain between RoguePlanet, ShieldBreak, and ShieldCrash is the clearest DFIR signal in this cluster. RoguePlanet is a Defender race condition yielding a SYSTEM shell. ShieldBreak bypasses the RoguePlanet fix targeting the same underlying workflow on Windows Server 2025. ShieldCrash then demonstrates arbitrary protected-file read as SYSTEM after the ShieldBreak remediation. A "patched" status against CVE-2026-50656 does not resolve exposure to CVE-2026-69414, and ShieldCrash represents a further distinct capability. Tracking the affected workflow and component version matters more than a product-level patch check.
- BlueHammer, RedSun, and UnDefend appeared in a documented intrusion. Investigators recorded unsuccessful elevation attempts and successful termination of UnDefend. The operators are not linked to Naceri. That incident is the artifact DFIR teams should anchor on: a failed elevation is not a contained intrusion. Investigate the originating account, parent process, remote-access session, and staging directory regardless of whether the tool succeeded.
- BigDiskBuster targets Defender update availability by monitoring update-related directories and attempting large temporary allocations during the update workflow. Files use delete-on-close behavior, meaning they may be gone by the time an analyst reviews the host, leaving normal free-space readings. Update failures and storage telemetry rather than current disk state are the relevant forensic surface. An endpoint agent can remain running while its platform or security intelligence goes stale, a gap that may not surface in agent-health dashboards without independent monitoring.
- Naceri alleges his Microsoft work account and MSRC database access remained active for two months after he was notified of dismissal. He states he did not retrieve or modify data. The claim raises an access-control question during the separation period. Resolving it requires authentication logs, repository access records, and precise timeline alignment between the September 2024 meeting, the March 2025 termination letter, and the June 30, 2025 contractual end date. This is a direct example of why offboarding verification should cover active sessions and vulnerability-management system permissions, not just account disable status.
Practitioner action: Verify Defender engine and platform versions against each CVE's first-fixed version separately. Do not treat the RoguePlanet fix as covering ShieldBreak or ShieldCrash. For BigDiskBuster exposure, retain historical update-event logs and storage telemetry independently of the endpoint agent. Correlate persistent update failures with large temporary file creation and unfamiliar processes from user-writable locations. Full IOC context, tool-specific prerequisites, and vendor remediation milestones are in the ThreatMon report.

item.title: Operation Master: Deconstructing a Multi-Tiered Intrusion and Monetization Pipeline
item.description:
Operation Master exposed: a single Brazilian 🇧🇷 threat actor ran a full intrusion-to-fraud pipeline, exploiting CVE-2026-0257 across 7 GlobalProtect gateways in four countries, stealing 600+ companies' data, then weaponizing it inside an automated multi-tenant invoice fraud platform that generated 2.4M+ messages and R$150.4M in attempted PIX fraud.
- CVE-2026-0257 (GlobalProtect authentication bypass) was the primary at-scale access vector. The actor forged auth cookies from target certificate context and fed candidates through a 30-worker automated exploit loop driven by continuous masscan output across 277.5M scanned hosts. The same CVE is being exploited separately by ransomware actors including Qilin, making it a high-priority patch target. Beyond VPN access, parallel campaigns hit SQLi targets via sqlmap and xp_cmdshell chains to pivot from database access to host execution, with DNS subdomain tunneling (470,268 queries from a single compromised host, structured as task.row.chunk.base64.x.random.victim-hostname) as the primary exfil rail, and rclone syncing to MEGA as a redundant second channel. Staged webshells (beacon.dll, wmsvc.dll, gopher_new.exe) and AdaptixC2 on 91.92.241[.]187 (ports 8443/4444/4321) provided C2 over HTTP and raw TCP. Additional techniques: SAM/SYSTEM/SECURITY hive theft (T1003.002), ntds.dit recovery (T1003.003), GodPotato token impersonation, PwnKit (CVE-2021-4034), CVE-2024-1086, and CVE-2023-7028 (CVSS 10.0 GitLab dual-email reset) hardcoding cyberkill2025[@]gmail.com as the attacker-controlled recovery address.
- The fraud monetization layer is a Node.js multi-tenant "master-panel" at /opt/master-panel/, running under PM2, backed by PostgreSQL and SQLite, and exposed externally on yzs[.]fi. Lookalike domains igreenfaturas[.]to, wattiofaturas[.]com, and nuvfaturas[.]com hosted per-victim invoice pages with URL parameters embedding the victim's real name, due date, consumption, and billing amount pulled from stolen utility databases. Email delivery routed through 12 hijacked M365 mailboxes (retail, healthcare, education) to inherit sender reputation. SMS ran across 8 SMPP gateways. PIX payments routed through a serverless Vercel proxy at pix-proxy-sable.vercel[.]app. The lead source was 1.8M records scraped via a passwordless JWT flaw in iGreen Energia's API. The fraud engine logged 622,666 personalized links, 317,696 click events, and R$38.9M in fraudulent invoices opened by victims.
- Attribution converges on forum persona masterblack and primary email cyberkill2025[@]gmail.com, which appears across: 34 fraud panel lead test records, the GitLab CVE-2023-7028 exploit hardcoding, OSINT API registrations (Shodan, VirusTotal, SecurityTrails, WPScan, AlienVault OTX), a recovered pentest report listing the operator, and a leaked hacker forum database record directly linking the email to the masterblack account that sold stolen iGreen and Wattio data weeks before the fraud campaigns began. The two-stage strategy, sell the data first, then phish the same victims with their own billing records, is confirmed by the 9 to 14 week gap between forum sale listings and bulk tenant seeding. The operator's AI agent workspace (36+ offensive subagents, ~45 persistent memory files) was exposed via a misconfigured cloud backup reachable from the first exploitation server at 85.120.216[.]8.
- Key detection opportunities from the article: sqlservr.exe spawning cmd.exe or PowerShell is a high-fidelity signal for the xp_cmdshell chain. High-entropy DNS queries from database service identities indicate active tunneling. rclone or unauthorized cloud-sync binaries on servers warrant immediate investigation. OAuth device-code grants without corresponding enrollment events indicate T1598 phishing. Unauthorized reads of SAM, SYSTEM, SECURITY hives or ntds.dit by service accounts are critical alerts. For the fraud infrastructure specifically, URL parameters matching the schema ?ref=, venc=, v=, v0=, kwh= on lookalike utility domains are a structural indicator of the invoice fraud platform's output.
Full IOC table (IPs, domains, SHA-256 hashes for all beacon and agent variants, qTox IDs) and the complete MITRE ATT&CK mapping are in the SOCRadar report. Prioritize hunting for AdaptixC2 gopher agent artifacts (gopher_new.exe SHA-256 54caa256483876debd21c264bfc31bd96f925b2167f6d9358ab7ee0c87e6e37b, beacon.dll SHA-256 d566ccdd099b0decb7e7288c20097f34da2613e3ffe8c5acbc1a1d01b6fe217c) and block the four operation server IPs: 85.120.216[.]8, 91.92.241[.]187, 91.92.241[.]184, and 185.242.3[.]14.

item.title: A Closer Look at Malware From the Macfinger ClickFix Campaign, (Fri, Sep 25th)
item.description:
The Macfinger ClickFix campaign is delivering an unidentified macOS information stealer distinct from AMOS Stealer, actively targeting macOS 27.0 (Golden Gate) with a multi-stage shell script loader chain and websocket-based C2 exfiltration.
Key findings:
- The infection chain starts at the fake CAPTCHA domain hollow-badger-moasfraum[.]life, which clipboard-injects a Terminal command. That command pulls a shell script loader from hxxp[:]//45.131.215[.]56/8031e818c7a46?force=1, which then checks uname -m and fetches the architecture-appropriate Mach-O binary: arm64 from hxxp[:]//45.131.215[.]56/a7a11f95?force=1 or x86_64 from hxxp[:]//45.131.215[.]56/4e04813226b1b93?force=1. The C2 address is base64-encoded inside the loader script itself.
- Persistence is established via a LaunchAgent plist at /Users/[username]/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.softwareupdated.plist, executing a binary dropped at /Users/[username]/Library/Caches/com.apple.softwareupdate/SoftwareUpdate. The initial staging location is /Users/[username]/Library/Caches/com.apple.securityd/com.apple.periodic. item.title: The Stealer Factory: Unpacking a Python-Based MaaS Infostealer Builder
item.description:
A Python-based MaaS infostealer builder lets low-skill operators compile customized credential stealers with XOR-obfuscated webhooks, dual persistence, and anti-VM evasion baked in at build time.
Key findings:
- The builder ships as a nested archive (my new program called 2.rar containing TokenGrabberBuilder.zip) with a GUI that auto-installs dependencies via pip at runtime, stores the operator's webhook URL in webhook.txt in the working directory, XOR-encodes it with key 0x5A then Base64-encodes it before injecting it into the payload, and offers three output modes: Nuitka (compiles to native machine code, defeats uncompyle6 and decompile3), PyInstaller (recoverable .pyc, unpackable with pyinstxtractor), or raw stealer.py for manual deployment. The interface explicitly labels Nuitka as "slower, stronger AV evasion," making the evasion intent explicit in the product itself.
- The payload's _debug_check() function runs four pre-execution environment checks: IsDebuggerPresent() via ctypes, process-name blacklisting for VirtualBox/Xen/QEMU/Parallels artifacts via psutil, a disk-size heuristic that exits if total capacity is under 50 GB, and a PID-derived variable sleep to outlast sandbox timeouts. All sensitive strings, including registry paths, SQL queries, and API endpoints, are stored as Base64-plus-XOR blobs decoded at runtime into the _E dictionary, and high-risk imports are loaded lazily through getter functions rather than at startup.
- Persistence uses two independent mechanisms: a Registry Run key written to HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run under the deceptive name "WindowsUpdate," and an ONLOGON scheduled task created with creationflags=0x08000000 (CREATE_NO_WINDOW) with stdout and stderr redirected to DEVNULL. Both survive reboots independently, so removing one does not clean the infection.
- Data harvesting targets 17 Chromium-based browsers (Login Data, History, Web Data, Cookies via DPAPI and AES-256-GCM decryption), Firefox profiles (places.sqlite, cookies.sqlite in plaintext), Discord tokens via LevelDB scanning and regex with live validation against /api/v9/users/@me, Roblox .ROBLOSECURITY cookies validated before packaging, and Wi-Fi passwords via netsh wlan show profiles key=clear. All harvested material is assembled in memory as StolenData_USERNAME.zip using Python's BytesIO to avoid touching the filesystem, then POSTed to the XOR-decoded webhook URL.
- Three IOCs are listed in the report: MD5 hashes 610f0c65a3f8e88559f89ed90ea9ee5c and 429ed63ab3fbda8d22d0ac750ecfe8cc (Password-Stealer 006dba241) and 9ffe0e45c7a3f20e4481206c1c3b0854 (Trojan 006e632e1).
For response and hunting: query EDR and process logs for pip.exe spawned by non-development parent processes, creation of a Run key value named "WindowsUpdate" under HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run, and schtasks activity with ONLOGON triggers tied to Python interpreters. Recover webhook.txt from the working directory if the builder was run locally. For the payload, hunt for Python processes making outbound HTTP POST requests to webhook endpoints and accessing SQLite files under browser profile directories. Because the exfil ZIP is constructed entirely in memory, filesystem forensics will not catch it in transit. Focus on network telemetry, DNS, and proxy logs for POST traffic to Discord or unknown webhook infrastructure. Full IOC list is in the report.

item.title: Measuring MITRE ATT&CK detection coverage: what the percentage counts and what it hides
item.description:
ATT&CK coverage percentages are widely misread: a library figure counts rules in a catalog, not detections that actually fire in your environment, and ATT&CK v19's tactic split makes pre-v19 numbers incomparable without recomputation.
Key findings:
- Four distinct coverage types exist and only one matters operationally. Library coverage counts techniques with at least one rule in a vendor catalog. Deployed coverage counts rules installed and enabled in your SIEM or XDR. Collected coverage counts techniques whose required data sources are ingesting and passing quality gates (freshness, null-rate, field-semantics). Validated coverage counts only techniques where a deployed rule has proven to fire against a real or simulated execution. A vendor's headline number is almost always Library. The number that describes your defended environment is Validated. Conflating them is the core failure mode.
- Data quality gates at the source layer are where programs quietly lose ground. A log source can be technically ingested while schema drift or a rising null-rate makes every detection built on top of it unreliable. The article gives concrete examples: T1110 Brute Force requires identity provider auth logs (Okta, Microsoft Entra ID) passing their contract; T1059 Command and Scripting Interpreter requires EDR process telemetry with clean field semantics; T1071 Application Layer Protocol requires network sensor, proxy, and DNS logs. A technique whose required source fails its gates scores zero, same as a technique with no source at all.
- ATT&CK v19 (released 2026-04-28) changed the denominator. The former Defense Evasion tactic was split into two new tactics: Stealth and Defense Impairment. Any coverage percentage computed before that split describes a different taxonomy. Pre-v19 numbers cannot be compared to post-v19 numbers without re-mapping rules to the new structure, recomputing per tactic, and publishing the delta explicitly. Relabeling the old number is not a valid update.
- Time-to-coverage is an underused but measurable program health metric. Track the interval from technique or procedure publication (t0) to a detection deployed and proven to fire in production (t1). Measure median and P90 by technique class, since a commodity technique and a novel procedure carry meaningfully different response windows. This metric exposes pipeline maturity in a way a static coverage heatmap cannot.
Practitioner takeaway: before accepting any coverage number, ask three questions the article names explicitly: what is the denominator (prioritized threat-model set or full ATT&CK matrix), which log sources does the figure assume are collected and passing quality gates, and which ATT&CK version was it computed on. If any answer is unknown, the number describes a catalog, not a defended environment. Run your own five-step validation: inventory deployed rules, map to ATT&CK v19 technique IDs, confirm each required data source passes freshness and null-rate gates, prove each rule fires using Atomic Red Team, MITRE Caldera, or AttackIQ, then compute per tactic. ATT&CK Navigator supports the mapping; tools like CardinalOps and Prime Hunt reconcile claimed mappings against live Splunk, Elastic, or Microsoft Sentinel environments to surface the library-to-validated gap directly.

item.title: AI Helps Uncover MikroTrick Attack Chain in MikroTik RouterOS
item.description:
MikroTick chains two RouterOS SSH flaws for unauthenticated admin access, actively exploited in the wild before patches shipped, now on CISA KEV with a three-day remediation deadline.
Both CVEs are actively exploited. CISA added them to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on September 10, 2026.
- CVE-2026-67279 and CVE-2026-86060 form the MikroTrick chain against MikroTik RouterOS SSH. CVE-2026-67279 allows an unauthenticated client to open a session channel by triggering an SSH rekey during the authentication phase: RouterOS incorrectly skips to channel handling as if auth had already succeeded. CVE-2026-86060 is the privilege escalation half. RouterOS passes the username as a command-line argument to the login process before auth completes, with no sanitization. Sending "-2" as the username causes the login process to treat it as a file descriptor option pointing to fd 2, the attacker-controlled terminal channel. Setting a privilege mask of 655358 then grants full administrative rights. No password, no SSH key, no successful authentication required.
- The exploit was circulating before the patches existed. Logs collected from the MikroTik forum, Reddit, and direct CERT Polska reports all point to a consistent source IP: 82.192.72[.]4. In confirmed cases, the attacker pulled diagnostic files off compromised routers after gaining access. MikroTik's September 3, 2026 patch introduced two defensive tells in the code: login now rejects usernames starting with a hyphen or a space, and a hardcoded check watches for a privileged account named "ops" appearing spontaneously and auto-disables it, confirming the vendor knew exploitation was occurring.
- The log signature is unusually clear. Every exploitation attempt leaves the same two-line sequence: a failed login for the user "-2" followed immediately by the creation of a fully privileged "ops" account. That pattern was already appearing in forum posts from administrators who had no idea what they were looking at. If you have RouterOS devices with SSH exposed, search your auth logs for that exact sequence right now before doing anything else. A failed login that results in a new admin account is not a logging anomaly, it is evidence of compromise.
- AI-assisted patch diffing closed the disclosure gap to hours, not weeks. CERT Polska used GPT-5.5-cyber and GPT-5.6-sol via OpenAI's GTAC program alongside locally hosted open-weight models to build a lab of 40 virtual RouterOS instances spanning 24 versions. AI agents analyzed binaries, fuzzed out-of-order SSH protocol behavior, and monitored forums for spread. A public post on npratley[.]net identified the key SSH changes by September 4, under 24 hours after the patch dropped. The "-2" file descriptor trick was being discussed openly on Reddit and MikroTik's forum by September 5. The asymmetry CERT Polska flags is the real problem: reverse engineering is now dramatically cheaper and faster, but forensic cleanup and patch deployment still move at the old pace.
Responder action: pull SSH auth logs on every RouterOS device in your environment and grep for the username "-2" and for account creation events showing a new account named "ops." Both artifacts map directly to this exploit chain. Check for unauthorized diagnostic file exports as a post-compromise indicator. Patch to the versions MikroTik released September 3, 2026, prioritizing any device with SSH reachable from the internet. CISA's three-day deadline on these KEV entries reflects real, confirmed exploitation, not theoretical risk. Full advisory and IOCs are available in the CERT Polska report.

item.title: Beyond the ransomware: Tracking Storm-2570’s consistent tradecraft across deployments
item.description:
Storm-2570 is a cross-ecosystem ransomware affiliate deploying Qilin, DragonForce, Anubis, and BERT across critical sectors in the US 🇺🇸, UK 🇬🇧, Canada 🇨🇦, Spain 🇪🇸, and Netherlands 🇳🇱. Microsoft Threat Intelligence has tracked this actor since April 2025, and the key insight is this: the payload changes, but the tradecraft does not.
- Storm-2570 operates as a RaaS affiliate across multiple ecosystems simultaneously, giving it flexibility to shift between operators while maintaining identical post-compromise behavior. Victims span healthcare, education, government, financial services, energy, critical manufacturing, and more. The actor renames MeshAgent binaries with victim organization names (e.g., meshagent64-[orgname].exe) and uses Base64-encoded commands through MeshCentral to evade cursory process review. NinjaRMM, Atera, ScreenConnect, Splashtop, and Remotely_Agent round out a deep bench of RMM tools deployed in the same intrusion, not as alternatives but as layers.
- Persistence and covert access are maintained through Cloudflare Tunnel (Cloudflared.exe) configured as a LocalSystem service, providing an encrypted outbound channel that bypasses inbound firewall restrictions. ngrok exposes TCP 3389 for RDP, and rdp.bat modifies Terminal Server registry settings and adds a firewall rule allowing port 3389, often pushed via PsExec with host lists (@ip.txt) to reach newly scanned targets. This combination of tunneling plus RDP enablement scripts plus PsExec with host lists is one of the most consistent fingerprints in the actor's chain.
- Credential access follows a predictable pattern: Mimikatz, LaZagne, and pypykatz for in-memory harvesting, plus ntdsutil to create an IFM backup of the Active Directory database, staging NTDS.dit and supporting registry hives under C:\Windows\Temp\[random] for offline hash extraction. This confirms domain controller access before ransomware deployment. Defense evasion precedes encryption: Storm-2570 disables real-time monitoring, adds Microsoft Defender exclusions for C:\PerfLogs, and modifies registry values under Defender service keys including DisableAntiSpyware, DisableRealtimeMonitoring, and WinDefend service entries.
- Exfiltration uses s5cmd.exe (Amazon S3 compatible CLI) staged alongside a credentials file containing AWS access keys, executing run cp operations with file-extension filters to push documents, spreadsheets, databases, mail files, and archives to attacker-controlled S3 buckets. Rclone handles real-time sync throughout the intrusion. This double-extortion workflow means data is already leaving before encryption begins. Lateral movement ties it together with Impacket and NetExec over SMB, PsExec across ip.txt host lists, and MeshAgent pushed to newly compromised hosts.
- Microsoft Defender for Endpoint detections to know: "Ransomware-linked threat actor detected", "Suspicious Atera activity", "Renaming of legitimate tools for possible data exfiltration", "Defender detection bypass", and "Process memory dump". Antivirus signatures cover HackTool:Win32/Mimikatz, HackTool:Win32/LaZagne, Ransom:Win32/Qilin, Ransom:Win32/DragonForce, and Ransom:Win64/Anubis among others.
Hunt now in Microsoft Sentinel using the two KQL queries in the report: one targeting PsExec command lines containing @ip.txt, and one hunting renamed MeshAgent binaries across DeviceProcessEvents, DeviceFileEvents, and DeviceRegistryEvents. Prioritize any environment where Cloudflared.exe runs as a LocalSystem service alongside MeshAgent variants with org-themed names. Enable tamper protection and DisableLocalAdminMerge immediately to block the Defender exclusion abuse. Full detection list and hunting queries are in the report.

item.title: One Tap Too Far: Using Shortcuts to Bypass Chrome for iOS Call Prompts
item.description:
CVE-2026-13795: A single tap on a malicious webpage bypassed Chrome for iOS call-initiation protections by routing tel: through Apple Shortcuts as a callback, triggering phone calls without user confirmation.

- The Chromium fix (issue 476591032, change 7838361) moves the prompt to the first handoff: Chrome now alerts before opening any shortcuts:// or workflow:// URL, covering x-success, x-cancel, and x-error in one stroke.

item.title: Detection Validation and Decay
item.description:
Detection rules marked "enabled" are not detection rules that work. Silent rule decay kills coverage without touching your dashboard, and most teams have no systematic way to find it.
- The core problem: a rule that parses cleanly, executes against an empty result set, and returns zero matches looks identical to a quiet-but-healthy rule from the SIEM's perspective. The dashboard stays green. No error fires. Five mechanisms cause this: log source version changes, field deprecation, field rename or retype, parser breakage dropping events to dead-letter queues, and source decommission. The textbook case is Windows Event 4688 where command-line content is only populated when a separate GPO setting is enabled. Disable or lose that policy on a gold image rebuild and every command-line detection silently stops matching.
- Four signals catch broken rules: fire-rate baselining against each rule's own recent baseline (Splunk index=_internal / index=_audit, Sentinel SentinelHealth table, Elastic Security Monitoring tab 8.x+), canary event injection end-to-end through the pipeline, periodic replay of stored positive samples, and schema-drift monitoring on required fields via null-rate trends. No single signal is sufficient.
- Retirement requires four inputs before removing a rule: fire history over the review window, ATT&CK technique mapping, coverage overlap assessed as technique-plus-data-source (not technique alone), and data source status.

item.title: Is This A Joke? In The Auth Header? (F5 BIG-IP UnAuth Heap-Overflow to RCE CVE-2026-94127)
item.description:
F5 BIG-IP APM heap overflow CVE-2026-94127 allows unauthenticated RCE via an oversized Authorization header. Actively exploited in the wild before patch release on Sept 22, 2026.
Key findings:
- The root cause is a missing bounds check in tmm64 (the F5 traffic management microkernel). A 0x4100-byte heap buffer is allocated for the OAuth userinfo flow, but the unpatched code copies the Authorization header value directly into that buffer without validating length first. A GET to /f5-oauth2/v1/userinfo with a Bearer token exceeding 0x4100 bytes triggers heap corruption, overwriting a function pointer at buffer+0x4ff8 and redirecting execution. No authentication required.
- Exploitation works despite ASLR and NX because tmm64 has no PIE (base 0x400000), giving stable gadget addresses. A stack pivot chains into a ret2plt execvp call. SELinux blocks exec syscalls, so the bypass appends commands to /etc/bigstart/scripts/tmm.finish, a hook Bash script that runs automatically when tmm crashes, turning the crash itself into the execution trigger.
- Affected: BIG-IP APM 21.x (21.1.0) and 17.x (17.1.0-17.5.1). Fixes are in Hotfix-BIGIP-21.1.0.2.0.30.22 and Hotfix-BIGIP-17.1.3.5.0.41.14. Other BIG-IP modules and BIG-IQ have no fix listed.
- Detection artifacts: look for tmm process crashes in /var/log/tmm, unexpected writes to /etc/bigstart/scripts/tmm.finish, and oversized Authorization headers in access logs on the /f5-oauth2/ path.

item.title: Hunting Invisible Unicode in Emails (+ KQL Queries)
item.description:
Invisible Unicode characters in email subjects and sender display names can silently bypass string-matching detections while leaving the rendered message visually unchanged to the human reader.

The user sees nothing different; a parser or security product may see a completely different string, undermining keyword-based detections and potentially manipulating AI email agents that process extracted text rather than rendered HTML.
- The hunting approach targets EmailEvents in Microsoft Defender XDR via KQL, extracting suspicious characters from Subject and SenderDisplayName using extract_all with the Unicode ranges above, then building a composite risk score: +40 for Unicode symbols/icons in subject (U+2600-U+27BF), +20 for hidden Unicode in subject, +20 for hidden Unicode in SenderDisplayName, +20 for multi-country sender infrastructure.
- The query retains NetworkMessageId and RecipientEmailAddress, making it suitable as a Defender XDR Custom Detection rule, not just a one-time hunt. Output is sorted by RiskScore descending so the highest-signal emails surface first.
Takeaway: Run the full KQL from the report against your EmailEvents table. A non-zero RiskScore is a hunting lead, not a verdict.

item.title: OAuth Token Theft Through Microsoft's Front Door | Huntress
item.description:

Key findings:
- The attack chain requires Developer Mode enabled (HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\AppModelUnlock, AllowDevelopmentWithoutDevLicense=1) or an enterprise AllowAllTrustedApps sideloading policy. Once set, a standard user runs Add-AppxPackage -Register with no UAC prompt. The AppX manifest declares WindowsRuntimeAccess="all" in ContentUriRules, granting attacker-hosted JavaScript full WinRT API access inside a trusted Microsoft process.
- The JavaScript calls the legacy WebAuthenticationBroker using Microsoft Office's own client ID (d3590ed6-52b3-4102-aeff-aad2292ab01c) and an oob redirect URI. The user sees a real login.microsoftonline[.]com dialog, completes MFA, and the auth code returns directly to the attacker. The captured token carries the full Office delegated scope set: Mail.ReadWrite, Files.ReadWrite.All, Teams, Directory.Read.All, and AuditLog.Create.

item.title: Digital Forensics: Deep Analysis with Plaso
item.description:
Plaso super-timeline construction from NTUSER.DAT, Windows Event Logs, and disk images gives investigators full-system visibility when SIEM and Sysmon are absent.
Key details:
- Plaso (log2timeline) is a Python-based timeline engine that ingests heterogeneous sources, NTUSER.DAT registry hives, .evtx files, syslog, and EnCase E01 disk images, into a single .plaso storage file, then exports to CSV via plaso-psort for analysis. Use plaso-pinfo to confirm event counts before export.
- NTUSER.DAT parsing is the highest-value starting point: the hive records USB connections, recently accessed folders, typed paths, and program execution history per user. Running log2timeline directly against the hive extracts the full user-activity timeline without needing a mounted volume.
- For large evtx datasets, narrow scope with a date filter in plaso-psort: "date > '2026-02-01 00:00:00' AND date < '2026-03-01 00:00:00'" to reduce noise and focus on the incident window rather than sorting tens of thousands of events blind.
- Full-disk imaging via E01 lets log2timeline sweep all supported artifact locations in one pass, producing a super-timeline that correlates across log sources and closes gaps left by missing enterprise logging.
When logging infrastructure is absent, run log2timeline against NTUSER.DAT first to establish user-activity baseline, then layer in System.evtx and a full E01 pass.

item.title: Process Parameter Poisoning: Inside a Novel EDR Evasion Technique
item.description:
Process Parameter Poisoning abuses undocumented Windows STARTUPINFO fields to inject shellcode into foreign processes, achieving zero EDR alerts in lab testing by avoiding all monitored memory APIs.
Key findings:
- The technique hides shellcode inside STARTUPINFO->lpReserved (or WindowTitle, CommandLine, Environment entries) before calling CreateProcessW(), bypassing VirtualAllocEx(), WriteProcessMemory(), and MapViewOfFile2() entirely. The payload lands in RTL_USER_PROCESS_PARAMETERS->ShellInfo.Buffer inside the new process's PEB, never touching the APIs EDR hooks watch. MITRE T1055, T1055.003, T1564.010.
- Execution flows through NtQueryInformationProcess() to locate PebBaseAddress, NtReadVirtualMemory() to read RTL_USER_PROCESS_PARAMETERS, a memory permission change to PAGE_EXECUTE_READ, then GetThreadContext()/SetThreadContext() to redirect the instruction pointer. No explicit suspend/resume APIs are called, so rules keyed to those calls miss it.
- Flashpoint validated a Rust POC with custom shellcode (no NULL bytes, no self-modifying encoders). Combined with DLL unhooking and the non-Microsoft block DLL policy on the sacrificial process, no XDR alerts or blocks fired.
